scenario: AITA for asking my pregnant SIL to leave the family Christmas gathering? | Okay so based on title I totally sound like an asshole but hear me out. So this year is our turn to host the family Christmas party at our home. We invited not only my SOs side but also my side as well. Overall it was around 20ish people in our home today for gift giving and typical American Christmas celebrating. Drinks were shared, food broken, the whole shebang. Amongst my SOs side of the family was his pregnant sister. She, I think, was due maybe a week or so ago? But really its just been ticking time bomb for her little one to arrive. Everybodys excited to meet the baby! Now our problem is that SIL came to the party with contractions and was obviously in labor (I know this because Im a mom myself - once you know, you know). Every 20 minutes or so she would start having pains and would make noises to pass the contractions. At first it wasnt so bad; I understand how sucky it is and you dont want to go to the hospital too soon because they'll just send you right home. But then it became almost obnoxious. I feel terrible for saying that but it really was. A lot of my family members and some of hers were glancing around like WTF? Go home and do that in private. After a while it became apparent that it was making everybody uncomfortable and even my MIL reccommend that she rest at home before it gets too late. She refused and said she was fine. In the middle of the kids opening their presents she went into pain again and this time she even screamed for a second. I then discreetly pulled her husband to the side and told them to leave. I did it politely ("Hey I appreciate you guys for being here but I think its time to go. I dont want you guys to give birth in our kitchen! lol"). After I said that her husband got angry and quickly got her and the kids packed up. She visibly upset and before heading out called me a bitch and said that I ruined Christmas for her. A few of their sides family members gave me dirty looks and left soon after. Im torn on this: I wanted everybody to have a good day but it was very distracting and obnoxious to have her around. I feel bad but still. tl;dr -- I asked SIL to leave family Christmas party because she was in labor.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it was right or wrong for this person to ask their pregnant sister-in-law to leave the family Christmas gathering. Let me start by understanding the situation better. So, the family was hosting a Christmas party with around 20 people. It was a typical celebration with gifts, food, and drinks. The sister-in-law (SIL) was pregnant and due any day. She came to the party, but it turned out she was in labor. The person who asked her to leave is a mom herself, so she recognized the signs of labor. At first, the contractions weren't too bad, but as time went on, they became more frequent and more noticeable. The SIL was making noises as she tried to pass the contractions, which started to make people uncomfortable. Even the mother-in-law suggested she rest at home, but she refused. Then, during the kids' gift opening, she screamed in pain, which was a bit much. The person then asked her to leave, politely, saying they didn't want her to give birth in their kitchen. Her husband got angry, they packed up, and she left, upset and calling the person a bitch. Some of their family members also left, giving dirty looks. So, the question is: Was it right or wrong to ask her to leave? First, I need to consider the feelings and perspectives of everyone involved. The SIL was in labor, which is a very personal and intense experience. She probably didn't want to leave the party, especially since it was a family gathering, and she might have been excited to meet her new niece or nephew. On the other hand, the host was trying to manage a party with 20 people, and having someone in labor in the middle of it was disruptive and uncomfortable for everyone. I think it's important to balance empathy with practicality. The host wanted everyone to have a good time, and having someone in labor in the kitchen is not ideal. It's also a safety concern—pregnancy and labor can be unpredictable, and having medical professionals nearby is important. The host was trying to prevent an emergency situation in their home. However, asking someone to leave during a family gathering, especially when they're in a vulnerable state like labor, is tough. It's easy to see why the SIL was upset and why some family members might have taken offense. The host's approach was polite, but it still felt like a harsh decision. I wonder if there was a middle ground. Maybe suggesting she take a break in a quiet room, or offering to call an Uber for her to go home without making a big scene. It's possible that the host could have handled the situation in a way that was less confrontational but still addressed the disruption. On the other hand, the SIL was making noises that were distracting and uncomfortable for others. It's reasonable for the host to want to maintain a pleasant environment for everyone. It's a tough spot to be in, balancing the needs of the group with the needs of an individual. I also think about cultural and personal expectations around family gatherings. In some cultures, family is everything, and asking someone to leave might be seen as disrespectful. In others, maintaining the comfort of the majority is more important. The host's decision might have been influenced by these cultural norms. Another angle is the legal and medical aspect. If someone is in labor, they should be in a hospital or a safe environment with medical care. The host was trying to prevent a home birth, which could have been risky. So, from a safety standpoint, asking her to leave might have been the responsible thing to do. But again, the way it was handled could have been better. Maybe the host could have communicated more gently or offered support instead of directly asking her to leave. It's a delicate balance between asserting control over the gathering and showing empathy towards someone in a difficult situation. In the end, I think the host's intention was to ensure the safety and comfort of everyone, including the SIL. However, the execution of the decision might have been insensitive. It's a tough call, and I can see both sides of the argument.
